thesis: This episode argues that investors should back founders with exceptional clarity and grit, particularly in high-risk, capital-intensive sectors like aerospace, where the science risk is low because the technology already exists. It emphasizes that 'hot' consumer companies often allow early investors to hold small stakes (sub-10%) while still capturing significant value, and highlights specific market leaders like DoorDash and Uber as examples of scalable businesses with distinct advantages.

claims.claim: Doodash is a food delivery company known to investors, similar to Instacart.

claims.claim: Blake is a founder focused on building a supersonic jet, and the science risk for Boom is low because the jet was already built.
claims.quote: Often at YCA, I often say, like, it goes back to the prior insight that I told shared with you, which is I don't think any other investor firm has that, which is we have this unique insight into how the founders are scaling and how big their vision or mission is. And Blake is that kind of a founder.

claims.claim: The science risk for Boom was very low because the supersonic jet was already built and there was a plane that launched.
claims.quote: The science risk for boom was very low. The supersonic jet was already built. And so there's proven science. It flew. What most people don't realized the reason they had to shut down Concord was it was not economically viable the way they built it.

claims.claim: The engineering risk for Boom is the bet being taken because the team's core strength is in software and attracting strong software folks.
claims.quote: Engineering risk is the bet we are taking. which is you have all this advancement, but the advancement really matters only in the speed and pace with which you execute and the less errors you can make.

claims.claim: The market and commercialization risk for Boom is low because Richard Branson was excited and they have contracts from commercial airlines.
claims.quote: Market of commercialization risk, like I remember when he was going through the batch, one of our group partners told him, go prove to me. I know you were not going to build this, but go prove to me that you can get Richard Branson excited about this. And he did it.

claims.claim: The funding risk for hot tech is different because there are plenty of pools of capital to tap into, including suppliers that finance the program.
claims.quote: So when you look at funding risk for hot tech, you have to think different. We're not assuming that this is venture capital that's going to fund them forever and see them through. But if you actually spend a lot of time in aerospace, you realize that the pools of capital that they can tap into are plenty.

claims.claim: The market risk for Boom is low because if the thing flies, there will be enough appetite from airlines and consumers.
claims.quote: When we did all the risk assessment, it was literally market risk is low. If the thing flies, there will be enough appetite from airlines and consumers.

claims.claim: DoorDash is the market leader in food delivery and there is room for two or three players in the market.
claims.quote: Today, undoubtedly, DoDash is the market leader. And there's still room for two or three players. And so what was different? One, the insight they had, they started from the suburbs.

claims.claim: DoorDash differentiated and scaled due to insights about starting in suburbs and focusing on merchant selection and workflow integration.
claims.quote: And those two insights alone is really what helped Doradge differentiate and scale. So in 2016, I remember this very vividly because that's when Uber Eats launched. And Uber is such a big right-sharing business.

claims.claim: DoorDash has a cost advantage in acquiring drivers compared to right-sharing companies like Uber.
claims.quote: It's actually, they are way more cost-deficient to acquire that driver, like 10 times better than what a right chan company does in terms of acquisition of driver. And you see that in their retention cohorts too.
